summary: Describes a strategy for resisting the Million Message Attack on the Cryptographic Message Syntax, where an attacker sends many chosen messages to learn a private key. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A thief might try a million guesses against a lock and learn how it works from the clicks. This describes ways to make that guessing game useless.

questions: how to prevent million message attack on cms
what is the million message attack
subtitle: How to stop an attacker from using a mail list server as an oracle to decrypt RSA-protected keys.

tldr.problem: The Million Message Attack lets an attacker recover a PKCS-1 encrypted block by sending about 2^20 modified messages and watching how the receiver reacts, and it also works against CMS.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver must react identically to all failure cases, ideally by substituting a random content-encryption key when the padding is bad, or by using OAEP padding.
tldr.outcome: Uniform behavior or random filling removes the signal the attacker needs; OAEP is not susceptible but is incompatible with PKCS-1.

today: RFC 3218 is Informational and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes OAEP as the upgrade path away from PKCS-1 padding.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
RSA encryption pads data out to the length of the modulus, typically 512 to 2048 bits, and the most popular technique is PKCS-1 version 1.5. In 1998 Bleichenbacher described an adaptive chosen ciphertext attack on SSL, called the Million Message Attack (MMA). It recovers a single PKCS-1 encrypted block if the attacker can convince the receiver to act as a kind of oracle, a program that answers queries using information the requester lacks, here the private key.

The MMA is also possible against CMS. Mail list agents are the most likely CMS targets, because they are automated servers that respond to many messages.
sections.eli5: If a guard answers differently when a guess is nearly right, a thief can use the answers to work out the secret. This memo is about guards that answer the same way every time.

sections.title: PKCS-1 Padding
sections.content:
In CMS, the thing being RSA-encrypted is a symmetric content-encryption key (CEK), anywhere from 8 to 32 bytes. It is placed in an encryption block the size of the modulus. The first byte is zero and the second is the block type, 2 for encryption. Then come non-zero random padding bytes, a zero byte, and the message.

There must be at least 8 bytes of non-zero padding. This stops an attacker from checking whether two encrypted keys are equal, because there are at least 255^8 (about 2^64) padding values, and from checking guessed keys by trial encryption.
sections.eli5: Before locking a secret in the box, you wrap it in a lot of random packing material, so two identical secrets never look the same.

sections.title: How the Attack Works
sections.content:
The attacker captures a ciphertext C and generates integers S, then computes C' = C*(S^e) mod n and sends it to the victim. Decrypting gives some M'. Most M' look like garbage, but about one in 2^16 starts with the correct 00 02 bytes and so appears properly formatted. Finding values of S that produce well formatted results reveals information about the original message. Operationally the attack usually needs about 2^20 messages and responses.

Because of the volume, only an automated victim is a realistic target. The attacker must also tell apart a badly formatted M' from the other outcomes, which could be bogus CEK, failed integrity check, or an apparently fine message. This can happen if the victim returns different errors or if timing differs. If the victim responds uniformly to all of these errors, no attack is possible.
sections.eli5: The thief sends a million slightly changed copies of the locked box and listens for whether the guard says "that looks right". Each answer leaks a tiny hint.

sections.title: Countermeasures
sections.content:
Careful checking of padding, CEK length and parity bits, with identical responses to every error, raises the number of probes needed. Done together, the three checks make the attack impractical, but each alone only increases the workfactor.

Random filling is the simplest fix. When the message is improperly formatted, the victim substitutes a randomly generated CEK of appropriate length and carries on. Later it fails with a decryption or signature error, exactly as it would for a properly formatted message with a wrong CEK. This also hides timing differences. Using a fixed CEK is a mistake, because the attacker could build a message with that CEK; the substitute should be cryptographically random.

OAEP padding is not susceptible to the MMA, but is incompatible with PKCS-1, so S/MIME and CMS must keep using PKCS-1 to talk to widely deployed implementations. OAEP is being specified for AES keys in CMS, giving an upgrade path.
sections.eli5: The best guard never reveals whether a guess was close. If something looks wrong, the guard just hands over a random fake key and plays along.
